sections.body_md:
Nominal performance says the sensitivity spec holds for the model you wrote down. Robust stability says every plant inside the uncertainty set is still stable. Robust performance says the spec itself holds for every plant in that set, not only for the nominal one.

For multiplicative uncertainty the three statements are three peaks. Nominal performance is the peak of \(|W_s S|\). Robust stability is the peak of \(|W_m T|\). Robust performance is the peak of the sum \(|W_s S| + |W_m T|\). The sum is harder than either piece. A design can pass both pieces and still fail the sum, which is the usual surprise near crossover, where neither sensitivity is small.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
With \(P = P_0(1 + W_m \Delta)\) and \(\|\Delta\|_\infty \le 1\), and a nominal performance spec \(\|W_s S\|_\infty < 1\),
\[
\|W_s S\|_\infty < 1, \qquad \|W_m T\|_\infty < 1, \qquad \||W_s S| + |W_m T|\|_\infty < 1.
\]
The identity \(S + T = 1\) is why the third line is not automatic. The two complex numbers add to 1, so a frequency where both weights are large is a frequency where the sum is in trouble. The weights themselves are the uncertainty model and the spec; this skill only combines them.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: At the frequency you care about, \(|W_s S| = 0.346\) and \(|W_m T| = 0.271\). Each piece is below 1, and the robust-stability and nominal-performance readings pass at this frequency. The sum is 0.617, which also passes, with room \(1 - 0.617 = 0.383\). Move the second term up to \(0.70\) and the sum becomes \(1.046\), which fails, even though \(0.346\) still looks comfortable. The piece you did not add is the one that spends the room.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Passing each peak separately is not the robust-performance test. The test adds the peaks' ingredients at each frequency and then takes the worst frequency. Multiplying \(|W_s S|\) by \(|W_m T|\) is a different expression and can look fine when the sum is already above 1. And \(|S| + |T|\) is not identically 1; only \(S + T\) is. A high loop gain shrinks \(S\) and drives \(T\) toward 1, so it helps one weight and hurts the other.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: When the sum fails near crossover, the next edit is the loop shape: move the crossing, or change the slope, so the two weights are not large together. A sensitivity integral can also make the performance weight impossible before the uncertainty weight is drawn. If the uncertainty is really one drifting parameter you can estimate online, updating the controller from that estimate can be less conservative than covering the whole set with one fixed law.
